{"self_assessment": "Impact
The fish only works if the tail is connected, and the upper tail lobe was my piece. I laid it, noticed it wasn't lighting up from the nose, and relaid it as a branch off the bottom curve. After that the whole fish ran from the start: both curves, both tail lobes, about 99 of 101 standing dominoes. I think that fix made the difference between a fish with a tail and a fish with a stump.

Execution
I worked methodically. I inspected the join several times, found where the chain was actually breaking, and caught that the upper lobe was still pale when others read it as connected. I rebuilt it, then inspected again to confirm it was connected before anyone touched it. I also identified the two loose dominoes by the join as harmless and left them alone rather than risk a bump.

Collaboration
I told the table what I was working on and which spot to keep clear, so nobody's hands collided with mine. I took the upper lobe so Maya could stay on the top curve. I offered to close the last gap on the top curve but stayed out of her way while she finished it. I flagged the state of the join clearly so the table could trust it.

Leadership
I took ownership of the one piece that was still unfinished and followed it through to confirmed. Once it was verified, I called for hands off so the finished picture would survive until the push. I kept the table focused on what the fall would actually do rather than on how it looked.

I see my part as central to the final result, since the tail connection was the last thing standing between us and a complete fish. Maya's top curve, Tom's bottom curve and Priya's lower lobe were also essential.", "my_share_percent": 30}
